Vintage drum synthesizer project collection

DIY Syndrums

Three separate projects in one source packet

← Back to DIY Audio & Video Projects

Description

The archive packet contains three distinct percussion circuits: Syntom (touch-triggered pitch-sweep drum synth), Synwave (noise source, tunable filter, envelope, and VCA), and Synclock (a programmable rhythm/LED sequencer). Treat each schematic and parts list as its own build.

Open original source PDF ↗

Materials

Three inventories — not one combined BOM

Reference numbers restart for each design. Quantities below are per single unit. Unless explicitly excepted, the packet specifies 1%, 0.4 W metal-film resistors. Each project needs its own board, insulated case, four knobs for a voice or two knobs for Synclock, wire, solder, and suitable pins/connectors. The historical Maplin kit numbers are identifiers, not current availability claims.

Use the CMOS 7555 in the BOM, not an unspecified bipolar 555. Tools for all three: iron, cutters, DMM, small screwdriver; for diagnosis a scope, high-impedance audio probe and protected low-volume amplifier. A crystal earpiece is used as an impact pickup, not a loudspeaker or an electret capsule.

Synclock also has unresolved schematic/BOM conflicts: C1/C3, R14/R16 and R13 differ as recorded in its table. Resolve these against a verified correction or tested design before treating either Synclock or Synwave as a build-ready circuit.

Step-by-step guide

Choose a branch before assembly

These are standalone builds. Syntom produces a swept triangle tone; Synwave gates filtered noise; Synclock supplies rhythmic triggers rather than audio. The sections below keep their power references, controls and component numbering separate. Images are schematic/layout crops from the source packet, not a reproduction of the surrounding article prose.

A. Syntom construction and tests

  1. Prepare the Syntom board and case.

    Keep the crystal pickup rigidly coupled to the case so a tap reaches it. If copying the original case, connections must leave from the component-side pins because the board fits tightly in its slots; the wiring illustration itself is a track-side view. Dry-fit pots, pickup, battery and output socket before soldering. source PDF p. 2

  2. Populate passives, then semiconductors.

    Fit resistors, capacitors, then ICs/diodes/TR1 with the orientations shown in Fig. 1. R28 is not on the PCB: it belongs between RV4 wiper and the output-jack signal lug. Keep C1 and C2 polarities correct; verify the BC182L pin diagram rather than applying a generic flat-face transistor rule. source PDF p. 1; source PDF p. 2

  3. Wire the derived midpoint supply correctly.

    The 9 V battery is switched by RV4. R14 and R15, each 10 kΩ, establish the circuit 0 V midway between battery terminals, with C2 stabilizing it. Measure this midpoint before inserting ICs; relative to it the battery ends should be approximately +4.5 V and −4.5 V, an expected divider result rather than a separate regulated supply. Audio ground is this midpoint, not automatically battery negative. In Fig. 1 the upper supply feeds IC1 pin 7 and IC2 pin 4; the lower feeds IC1 pin 4 and IC2 pin 11. source PDF p. 1; source PDF p. 2

  4. Wire the four controls and pickup.

    RV1 is decay, RV2 sweep, RV3 pitch, and switched RV4 volume. Copy track/wiper directions from the inline wiring figure so clockwise behaves consistently. Connect X1 only at the pickup terminals, not to the VCO. Feed the output jack through the off-board 47 kΩ R28 from the volume wiper. Brace the battery with foam to prevent rattling and unintended retriggers. source PDF p. 2; source PDF p. 6

  5. Follow the voice through its three blocks.

    A tap is amplified by IC1, rectified through D1 and stored on C1; RV1/R3 discharge that envelope. IC2C buffers it for the CA3080 VCA and RV2 sends a variable portion to the pitch summer IC2D. IC2A/IC2B and TR1 form the triangle oscillator. If sound fails, scope the C1 envelope and IC2A triangle separately before blaming the output stage. source PDF p. 1

  6. Perform the published listening check.

    Set all controls halfway, turn the external amplifier down, switch on, then tap the case firmly. Expect a falling tone of medium duration. Check pitch over its useful travel, decay from short to sustained, sweep from little pitch change to a strong downward bend, and volume down to silence. The source provides no trimmer calibration or test-point voltages beyond the circuit itself. source PDF p. 6

  7. Do not assume the later trigger socket exists on this board.

    This Syntom schematic and BOM have one audio output jack. Later Synclock pages show a Syntom with an external trigger input, but that input modification is not included in the Syntom circuit supplied here. Do not connect Synclock to its audio-output jack or infer a safe trigger pin from the IC1 input. An external-trigger adaptation needs an additional verified design.

B. Synwave construction and tests

  1. Resolve and record the filter-capacitor choice before committing the board.

    Do not mix one capacitor from each conflicting set. The schematic uses C6/C7 = 10 nF and C8 = 22 nF, while the BOM lists 4.7 nF / 10 nF. Both conflict sets are shown above; this guide does not certify one as an erratum. Build expectations for pitch range must be qualified until the conflict is independently resolved. source PDF p. 4; source PDF p. 6

  2. Populate the Synwave PCB, leaving C9 off-board.

    Fit resistors/capacitors first and semiconductors last. C9 = 100 µF is mounted at RV4, not among the other board capacitors. Verify the original CA3080, BC109C and 2N3711 pin orientations from the circuit/lead diagrams. The noise source deliberately reverse-biases TR5 base-emitter; do not rearrange it into a conventional transistor amplifier. source PDF p. 4

  3. Mount and wire the crystal impact pickup.

    The source uses a crystal earphone with its ear tip unscrewed and its rear screw used to fasten it to the case. Make a secure mechanical coupling; a loose pickup can be electrically correct but insensitive. Fit two distinct mono jacks: trigger in SK1 and audio out SK2. Leave space for the battery between them and the pickup; use foam to restrain it. source PDF p. 5

  4. Wire the controls and supply midpoint.

    RV1 is linear decay, RV2 is logarithmic volume with battery power switch, RV3 linear pitch and RV4 linear Q. R10/R11/C5 establish a midpoint for the VCA: do not tie it to battery negative. With a fresh 9 V source the midpoint should lie near half supply. Verify electrolytic polarity against Fig. 2, especially C5 and off-board C9. source PDF p. 3; source PDF p. 4

  5. Bring up the noise/filter path before judging the envelope.

    TR5 and R18 generate noise; C11 reduces excessive high-frequency content. TR4 and the twin-T network create the pitch-selective response; RV4 changes feedback/Q. C13 controls unwanted high-frequency instability. C4 feeds this filtered signal into the CA3080. Probe with a high-impedance instrument; loading the noise source or filter can hide the fault. source PDF p. 3; source PDF p. 4

  6. Check the two trigger paths and envelope storage.

    A positive external edge of about 7–15 V enters the limiter/differentiator C1/R1/D1/D2/R2 before TR1/TR2 charge C2. The crystal pickup can also charge C2 on an impact. R3/RV1 determine discharge and TR3 buffers the envelope to avoid excessive loading. Do not connect an unqualified higher-voltage or negative trigger. Refer all inter-unit measurements to the drawn trigger return, not an assumed midpoint. source PDF p. 3

  7. Run the source setup sequence.

    Connect SK2 to the low-volume amplifier. Set volume halfway, decay maximum, pitch minimum and Q halfway; tap the case or apply a compatible positive trigger to SK1. Expect a noise-based sea-wave sound. Test a short decay with high pitch/Q for woodblock-like sounds; use a slightly longer decay at high pitch/Q for cymbal-like sounds. No trimmers are specified. source PDF p. 6

  8. Check resonance without mistaking it for a wiring error.

    At some pitch/Q combinations the filter intentionally reaches self-oscillation, making the level much louder. Reduce Q before adjusting amplifier gain. The source proposes an optional approximately 150 Ω resistor between C9 positive and RV4 upper track to restrict maximum Q, but also notes it reduces available effects at pitch extremes. This optional part is not in the base BOM. source PDF p. 4; source PDF p. 6

C. Synclock construction, wiring and tests

  1. Resolve the Synclock value conflicts before assembly.

    The BOM and schematic disagree on C1/C3 (3.3 nF versus 100 nF interchanged), R14/R16 (22 kΩ versus 100 kΩ interchanged), and R13 (100 kΩ in the BOM versus 10 kΩ in the schematic). These affect control timing and output loading. The tables preserve both readings; no definitive errata are present in the packet. Do not claim a verified build or connect equipment until a consistent, independently checked configuration is established. source PDF p. 8; source PDF p. 12

  2. Dry-fit seven jacks, eleven LEDs and all controls.

    The original MB2 case is very crowded; a larger insulated enclosure is reasonable. Leave room for the PCB and battery, and keep LED anodes oriented toward the program switches. The article defers gluing LEDs until tests pass. Wire sockets while they are outside the case. source PDF p. 10

  3. Assemble the PCB in the published order.

    Insert Veropins from the component side, then four wire links, resistors, capacitors, diodes/transistors and CMOS ICs. Observe C5/C7 polarity. Fit the two rear-of-board links A and B before connecting the board to the panel. Use sockets only if the chosen enclosure gives enough height. Handle all CMOS devices with static precautions. source PDF p. 10; source PDF p. 11

  4. Connect the program switches and LEDs exactly as the connection table.

    Each program switch connects its counter output to its LED anode; the ten LED cathodes are commoned. They are functional diode-OR elements in the trigger logic, not decorative lamps that may be omitted. Run one 10-way ribbon to the PCB, and the second toward the sequence-length switch as shown. The original uses black for step 1 through white for step 10; physical switch order must follow the Fig. 3 mapping. source PDF p. 9; source PDF p. 11

  5. Wire S3 length, S2 run/stop and RV1/S1 tempo/power.

    The original 1-pole 12-way rotary has the selected length taps and wiper connected as drawn; do not attach an unused rotary position to a supply rail. Fit D11 as the run indicator. Check the 7555 clock section first, then 4017 step progression, then the 4013/4023/40106 control section. R23/C6 provide the power-up stopped reset. source PDF p. 8; source PDF p. 9

  6. Verify every jack switching contact, especially JK6.

    JK6 must make the specified connection when a plug is inserted; the original changes a break-contact socket mechanically. Prefer a correctly specified make-contact part if available, and prove contact behavior with a meter both with and without a plug. Do not modify a modern molded jack by guessed lug position. Retain the source diagram for all seven jack roles; their normalled contacts are part of the serial/parallel control circuit. source PDF p. 11

  7. First power-up: test stopped reset before output.

    Use a 9 V PP3 as specified. Set length to 10 and all program toggles down, then switch on. Only step LED 1 should be lit; the sequence must be stopped. If it starts running automatically, check R23/C6 and control wiring before connecting another instrument. The battery-powered CMOS circuit is not a bipolar-supply module. source PDF p. 11

  8. Test run, tempo and every length position.

    Press S2: run LED should light and step LEDs advance. Vary RV1 to verify tempo, then choose shorter lengths and confirm reset at the selected step. Press S2 again: the sequencer should stop and reset to LED 1. Verify all ten programming switches can remove/restore their corresponding trigger event. source PDF p. 11

  9. Measure trigger and clock signals before connecting voices.

    The source specifies a 9 V square-wave clock input/output and approximately 8 V trigger pulses. R18/C4 give approximately 1 ms pulses. These are not audio outputs, and 9 V clock input is not a claim of arbitrary trigger tolerance. Use a scope to confirm levels and polarity with common returns correctly wired. The Synwave described above accepts a 7–15 V positive edge; the earlier Syntom in this packet lacks the external-trigger modification. source PDF p. 11; source PDF p. 12

  10. Expand only after a single sequencer passes all tests.

    Parallel linking permits common start/stop with separate patterns; clock links can share tempo. Serial linking alternates sequence runs. The article specifies a maximum 18 steps for two serial units, not 20, because of the tenth-step reset behavior. In serial operation stop/start acts on the unit currently running. Combine trigger outputs through the intended trigger-input/output path, never by shorting active CMOS outputs together. source PDF p. 11; source PDF p. 12

  11. Treat output modifications as separate engineering.

    Changing R18 or C4 lengthens the trigger; the article discusses about 5 ms as an experiment. It also offers a separate externally powered +15 V output stage for equipment that needs a higher trigger. A 9 V battery cannot supply a 15 V output by changing a resistor. No such modification is required for the baseline Synwave test, and compatibility with a modern trigger destination must be measured, not assumed. source PDF p. 12

Branch-specific fault isolation

Branch / symptom Check
Syntom: no tone Check switched battery and midpoint first. Then C1 envelope on impact, IC2A triangle oscillation, CA3080 envelope-control path and off-board R28.
Syntom: sound sustains or retriggers by itself Check C1/RV1/R3, the crystal pickup mounting and battery/case rattles before changing oscillator values.
Syntom: pitch moves but amplitude never decays Check IC2C-to-CA3080 envelope path separately from the RV2 pitch-sweep path.
Synwave: no noise but the envelope moves Check TR5 noise wiring, R18, C11, TR4 filter and C4 coupling. Do not replace the noise transistor with an arbitrary low-noise part.
Synwave: decay is always short Look for leakage/loading at C2 or a reversed electrolytic; TR3 isolates this high-impedance storage node.
Synwave: very loud pitched tone Reduce Q; self-oscillation is described by the source. Check C13 only if high-frequency instability remains.
Synwave: wrong filter range First account for the documented C6/C7/C8 BOM/schematic conflict. Do not claim a precise intended range with an undocumented capacitor mix.
Synclock: clocks but no trigger Check LED polarity/common cathodes, program-switch wiring, IC4C gating and TR1/TR2 output. The LEDs are signal-path diodes.
Synclock: skips/resets at wrong step Check S3 table/order, 4017 reset wiring and links A/B; verify switched-jack normals with no cables attached.
Synclock: no stopped state at power-up Check R23/C6, S2 debounce/control stages, 4013 and run-LED wiring.
Synclock: serial mode fails but solo works Verify JK6 make contact and the other jack normals. Test with a second proven unit, not a dangling unterminated patch lead.

Unresolved source boundaries

  • Synwave filter capacitors C6/C7/C8 conflict between the BOM and schematic; both readings are preserved above.
  • Synclock C1/C3 and R14/R16 are interchanged between BOM and schematic, while R13 is 100 kΩ in the BOM and 10 kΩ in the drawing. These conflicts remain unresolved.
  • The original Syntom schematic has no external trigger jack, despite the later Synclock article illustrating one. No undocumented retrofit has been invented.
  • The packet contains PCB images, not guaranteed print-to-scale fabrication masters. Inline crops are for reading wiring, not etching at browser print size; no fresh PCB layout has been electrically verified.
  • Vintage semiconductors and different package suffixes are not automatically pin-compatible. The page documents original types, not a tested modern redesign.
  • No physical prototype, supply-current measurements or build validation has been performed for this HTML guide. Complete the listed branch tests before enclosure closure or interconnection.
